title: Warriors who Protected Honour and Valour
paragraphs: The Puṟattiṇai chapter in Tolkāppiyam speaks of seven thematic situations (tiṇais) of Puṟam corresponding to the seven Akam situations. They are

1. Veṭci (counterpart of kuṟiñci) is the seizure of the cattle of an enemy king in secret by the vassals or officers of his rival (and taking the animals under the latter’s protection), an act provoking war in ancient times. The counter-attack in the form of fighting and recovery of the seized cattle by the enemy king’s men is also part of this tiṇai.

2. Vañci (counterpart of mullai) is the march of one king with his forces against another, causing fear to the subjects of the kingdoms; it is motivated by the ambition of seizing territory through conquest.
3. Uḻiñai (counterpart of marutam) is the siege by an attacking king of a fort, along with its defence by the king remaining within.

4. Tumpai (counterpart of neytal) is the heroic attack of the invading king met with equally heroic resistance in battle by the defending king. The focus here is on deeds of exceptional valour and heroism in battle performed by

warriors of either side in an attack; the tumpai situation can occur with other situations involving fighting, e.g., veṭcippuṟattumpai, dealing with exploits of bravery in cattle seizure preliminary to war.

5. Vākai (counterpart of pālai) is the excellence achieved by different social orders as well as sages and ascetics-in-penance, performing their functions by themselves and in complementation or confrontation with others.
6. Kāñci (counterpart of peruntiṇai) treats of the instability of human life, youth, wealth, etc.
7. Pāṭāṉ (counterpart of kaikkiḷai) speaks the praises of a male patron (āṇ) by a suppliant poet seeking the former’s benefaction.

> Veṭci is > Men at the border-posts, > Charged by their ruler, > Capturing the cows of the hostile king by stealth > And keeping them right under guard. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 2)

Coming to veṭci situation, there are fourteen types of activities (called sub-situations (tuṟais)) attendant on it. These activities in their order of occurrence are enumerated in Tolkāppiyam as under:

> The fourteen substrands of the veṭci theme are: > The clamour > That marks the army’s movement to lift the foeman’s cows; > The utterances of townsfolk around > Coming for good omens for the marching men; > The men’s march > Being unknown to the foeman’s spies > That infiltrate into their midst; > The marching men’s spying > Unnoticed by the foeman; > Lying in wait for the moment opportune to lift the cows > Encircling the foemen’s positions spied right; > Slaying of foemen that offer resistance; > Capturing the cows therein; > Putting to rout the foemen in pursuit; > Being back home

> With no affliction to the cattle captured; > Home that they are > To witness cheer and accolade; > Securing the herds of cows at home; > The cows captured being shared; > Revelry marking the victorious seizure of cows > And gifting away of cows to others too. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 3)

What is important here is not the victory or the defeat of one king or the other, but the acts of prowess and courage and honour displayed by the warriors of both sides. Here is a poetic illustration of Tolkāppiyar’s exposition in a Puṟanāṉūṟu poem (269) by Avvaiyār:

> Wearing a garland of wild jasmine full of seeds and a few blossoms and > buds as sharp-tipped as a kuyil’s beak resplendently bedecking our thick > black hair, you drank once, and again, of liquor as amber as a tiger’s eyes > poured out in a new cup, and then because a tuṭi drummer wearing a > chaplet of dried leaves and drumming the call to battle on his drum had > come, you refused to praise and accept the filtered, intoxicating toddy > they then offered you, but instead took up this sword, they say, into > your powerful hand and with it, after tracking bowmen who had seized > the many long lines of cattle in combat where the warriors wore > fragrant basil, you cut down those enemies while the red vultures > screeched, sailing on their curving wings!
